analysis.one_liner: Requires employer safety programs and worker safety committees, extends coverage to public employees, and raises penalties for violations.
analysis.headline: Despite hearings in 1993 and 1994, the bill never got a committee vote or a Senate floor vote, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the nation's workplace safety law. Every employer would have to maintain a written safety program; employers with 11 or more workers would have to set up joint safety committees with employee representatives who get paid time for inspections and meetings. It would extend federal safety coverage to state and local government workers and Department of Energy nuclear workers, speed up the process for setting limits on toxic exposures, require a standard on ergonomics, and sharply increase fines and prison terms for willful violations that injure or kill workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers would gain the most: employees at worksites with 11 or more workers would get a voice in safety through elected or union-designated representatives with rights to inspect the site quarterly, review injury records, and get written responses to their recommendations. Workers could refuse imminently dangerous work without being fired, and reporting an injury or unsafe condition would be protected against retaliation. Around eight million state and local government employees, who are currently outside federal OSHA coverage, would be brought under it, along with construction workers, who face some of the highest death rates, and Department of Energy nuclear workers. Families of workers killed or injured on the job would get new rights to information and participation in enforcement proceedings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Millions of workers, including state and local government employees

how_it_helps.text: Every employer would have to establish and carry out a written safety and health program identifying, documenting, and correcting hazards, with training provided at no cost to employees and counted as paid work time.

Employers with 11 or more employees would have to create joint safety and health committees including employee representatives chosen by the nonmanagerial workforce, with rights to quarterly worksite inspections, review of injury records, and timely written responses to their recommendations.
The bill extends OSHA coverage to state and local government employees and applies the Act to work performed in Department of Energy nuclear facilities.

Criminal penalties would be dramatically increased: prison terms for willful violations causing death would rise from one year to 20 years, a new crime would cover willful violations causing serious bodily injury even without death, and liability would extend for the first time to corporate officers, managers, and supervisors, whose fines could not be paid out of company assets.

Employees would gain an explicit right to refuse work identified as an imminent danger without discrimination, new protection for reporting injuries or unsafe conditions, and standing to contest settlements between OSHA and employers that withdraw citations.

The bill would require a final ergonomics standard to protect workers from musculoskeletal disorders, regular updating of toxic exposure limits on a three-year cycle, and a rule adopting the 1989 air contaminants limits within 60 days of enactment.

Construction sites would get dedicated oversight, including an Office of Construction Safety, targeted inspections of contractors with poor records, and mandatory reporting of fatalities and serious incidents.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the cost. Businesses with 11 or more workers would fund safety committees and paid time for training, meetings, and inspections; all employers would build and maintain written safety programs, exposure monitoring, and expanded recordkeeping. Larger fines and, for the first time, personal criminal liability for officers and supervisors would raise the price of violations. State and local governments would face new compliance obligations as covered employers. Some costs would reach consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, including small businesses and governments

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on all employers: written safety programs, paid committee time, paid training, exposure monitoring, and expanded injury recordkeeping. Small firms feel these fixed costs most heavily, and some of the cost would be passed to consumers in prices.

Criminal liability would extend to individual managers and supervisors with control over a workplace, not just the company, and prison terms for willful violations would rise to as much as 20 years; critics of the bill argued this would expose front-line managers to severe personal risk for workplace conditions they may not fully control.

The bill includes a concession to employers: a citation must be vacated if the employer shows workers were trained, rules were communicated and enforced, and employee misconduct caused the violation, giving companies a way to escape penalties by blaming workers.

Mandatory committees in the many worksites with no union would create a new standing employee body and administrative machinery that some employers would find burdensome, even though the bill specifies committees would be advisory and could not count as labor organizations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are real and the public stakes are large: workplace deaths, injuries, and illnesses were the bill's stated reason for action, and expanded coverage, faster standards, and stiffer penalties attack all three. The costs are also real but ordinary for safety regulation — paperwork, paid time, and monitoring — and the bill targets help and simplified alternatives at small employers. The employee-accountability escape valve is the weakest part, letting well-documented employers off the hook for violations caused by workers. On balance this is a significant transfer of bargaining power and protection toward workers, paid for mostly by employers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held hearings in July 1993 and again in February and March 1994, but it was never marked up or brought to the Senate floor, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy, chair of the Labor and Human Resources Committee, introduced the bill on March 11, 1993 with Senator Howard Metzenbaum, and it was read twice and referred to Kennedy's own committee.
Fourteen Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The committee held hearings in July 1993 and in February and March 1994, printed as S.Hrg. 103-334 and S.Hrg. 103-638, but never voted to report the bill to the Senate.

The bill's last recorded action was the March 22, 1994 hearing; it received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no House companion action in the record, and expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

The bill's findings state that millions of employees exposed to serious hazards were excluded from coverage and that enforcement had not been adequate to deter violations or force timely correction of dangerous conditions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off because the bill died: no mandatory safety programs or committees, no paid time for worker safety representatives, no extension of OSHA to state and local government workers, and no higher fines or personal criminal liability for officers and supervisors. The workers those provisions would have protected, including public employees still outside federal OSHA coverage, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who faced no new safety mandates

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as chair of the committee it was referred to, held hearings on it in 1993 and 1994.

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Joined Kennedy in introducing the bill on the first day it was filed.

for.name: 14 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Business and employer associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the OSHA overhaul, lobbying against mandatory safety committees, expanded coverage, and higher penalties; the bill never reached a floor vote in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 senators who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats, and the Senate record shows no Republican support; the bill was also never taken up by the House.

industries.note: Mandatory written safety programs, joint committees with paid employee representatives, exposure monitoring, expanded recordkeeping, and stiffer fines would raise operating costs. The industry's saving on these requirements came at the price of workers continuing to face the hazard levels the bill targeted.

Public agencies would become covered employers subject to federal OSHA standards, enforcement, and compliance costs for the first time. Their employees, among the millions excluded from coverage, would be the beneficiaries.

The bill created a construction safety office, a trained inspector academy, mandatory project safety plans, targeted inspections of contractors with bad records, and new enforcement duties for project constructors. Construction had among the highest fatality rates, so the cost fell on contractors with the worst safety performance.

industries.industry: Safety and health training and consulting
industries.note: Mandatory programs, committees, and training would create demand for compliance curricula, technical assistance, and safety resource centers the bill would fund through grants and an OSHA assistance fund.

industries.industry: Officers and supervisors of covered employers
industries.note: For the first time, individual managers with control over a workplace could face criminal charges and personal fines for willful safety violations, and those fines could not be reimbursed by the company. Their exposure would have risen sharply while workers gained a stronger deterrent against cutting corners.
